title: Three Millennia of Medical Ink: Clay, Papyrus, Silk & Amate on Trial

teenKit.tldr: While ancient skulls prove prehistoric surgeons successfully performed brain surgery, only fragile surviving texts like papyrus and clay tablets reveal the actual recipes, logic, and fierce medical debates behind how they saved lives.
teenKit.whyItMatters: Without written medical literature to pass down breakthroughs and explain the 'why' behind treatments, humanity would be trapped in an endless loop of relearning how to heal from scratch.
keyTakeaways: Bones can prove that an ancient person survived a brutal medical procedure like trepanation, but they cannot explain the treatment's logic.
Medical history is dangerously fragile because a single fire, flood, or forgotten language could wipe out centuries of life-saving knowledge overnight.
Ancient healing was a truly global enterprise, spanning thousands of years and utilizing diverse writing materials from Mesopotamian clay to Mesoamerican fig bark.

quiz.question: What is the major limitation of relying solely on ancient human bones to understand past medicine?
options: Bones dissolve completely within a few decades.
Bones only show what physical trauma occurred, not the medical logic, recipes, or intent behind the treatment.
Ancient humans never marked their bones with medical interventions.
Bones are too heavy to study in modern laboratories.
quiz.explanation: While bones show physical evidence like healed drill holes, they completely miss the instructions, dosages, and debates of the healers.

quiz.question: According to the episode, why were ancient medical texts considered dangerously fragile compared to bones?
options: They were written in invisible ink that faded after a century.
They could easily be destroyed by fire, water, or the loss of the language used to read them.
Ancient rulers intentionally burned all medical libraries every ten years.
They were carved onto blocks of ice that melted.
quiz.explanation: Organic writing materials like papyrus, silk, and paper can easily burn or rot, and knowledge vanishes if a language becomes a dead tongue.

options: The surgery happened post-mortem as a religious ritual.
The patient survived the procedure and lived long enough for their bone to grow back.
Ancient anesthetic drugs were completely painless.
The skull was accidentally damaged by falling rocks.
quiz.explanation: Bone only knits back together and smooths out over time in a living patient, proving the ancient operation was a success.
